title: The Manifold Adventure
introduction:
# Learn the structures Lean geometers actually use

Ada is an ant who can only inspect her world from the inside. That is exactly the point of manifold theory: global spaces are understood through local coordinate patches.

This version of the course works directly with **Mathlib's real manifold API**. The first goal already contains a `Homeomorph`; later worlds use `OpenPartialHomeomorph`, `ChartedSpace`, `atlas`, `chartAt`, `ModelWithCorners`, `IsManifold`, `TangentSpace`, and `TangentBundle`.

There are two kinds of names in your inventory:

- Names such as `Homeomorph.continuous` and `mem_chart_source` are **Mathlib declarations**. The course unlocks them when their mathematical meaning has been introduced.
- Names such as `homeomorph_continuous` and `tangent_zero` are **your course declarations**, defined in the `ManifoldAdventure` namespace. Propositions become theorems; constructed mathematical values become definitions. Both are reusable in later levels.

Every reference solution is compiled against pinned Mathlib source and checked by Lean's kernel. There are no course axioms, `sorry` declarations, or toy stand-ins for the manifold structures.

## Reading the notation

- `X ≃ₜ Y` is Mathlib notation for a homeomorphism.
- `x ∈ s` is typed with `\in`.
- `𝓝 x` is the neighborhood filter at `x`; type `\nhds`.
- `ℝ`, `∞`, and `ℕ∞` are Lean objects, not prose abbreviations.

Start with **Homeomorphisms**. The difficulty rises from field projection and theorem application to typeclass-driven constructions and dependent pairs.
information:
The formal source is `lean/ManifoldAdventure/BrowserBase.lean`. It imports `Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.IsManifold.Basic` at pinned Mathlib commit `de3a9cf33016bbb6d15880d7680643f7ca2d25ba`.

For the mathematics, continue with Loring Tu's *An Introduction to Manifolds*, John Lee's *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds*, or John Milnor's *Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint*.
caption: A kernel-checked path through Mathlib homeomorphisms, local charts, atlases, smooth manifolds, products, and tangent bundles.

worlds.title: Homeomorphisms
worlds.introduction:
# Same topology, different labels

A homeomorphism is not merely a function with a suggestive name. In Mathlib, `Homeomorph X Y`—written `X ≃ₜ Y`—contains an equivalence, a proof that its forward map is continuous, and a proof that its inverse is continuous.

This world teaches you to read a bundled mathematical structure. You will project facts from the bundle, use its inverse laws, and compose two homeomorphisms.

levels.title: Continuity is bundled
levels.introduction:
The hypothesis `e : X ≃ₜ Y` already stores the proof that its forward function is continuous. Mathlib exposes that field through the theorem `Homeomorph.continuous`, and dot notation lets you write it as `e.continuous`.

Use `exact` to supply that proof to the goal.
levels.conclusion: You just proved a theorem about Mathlib's bundled `Homeomorph` structure. No informal “looks the same” proposition was substituted for continuity.
levels.statement:
homeomorph_continuous {X : Type u} {Y : Type v} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (e : X ≃ₜ Y) : Continuous e
hints: The homeomorphism `e` has a theorem named `e.continuous`.

levels.title: The inverse is continuous too
levels.introduction:
A continuous bijection is not automatically a homeomorphism: the inverse must also be continuous. Mathlib records this separately as `Homeomorph.continuous_symm`.

The expression `e.symm` is itself the inverse homeomorphism, coerced here to its underlying function.
levels.conclusion: The forward and inverse continuity fields are why a homeomorphism preserves topology in both directions.
levels.statement:
homeomorph_inverse_continuous {X : Type u} {Y : Type v} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (e : X ≃ₜ Y) : Continuous e.symm
hints: Look for the inverse counterpart of `e.continuous`.

levels.title: There and back
levels.introduction:
Coordinates must not lose the point they describe. A homeomorphism sends `x` to `Y`; its inverse sends the result back to exactly `x`.

This is the genuine inverse law `Homeomorph.symm_apply_apply`, inherited from the equivalence inside the homeomorphism.
levels.conclusion: Round-trip equations are the algebraic heart of changing coordinates.
levels.statement:
homeomorph_round_trip {X : Type u} {Y : Type v} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (e : X ≃ₜ Y) (x : X) : e.symm (e x) = x

levels.title: Compose coordinate changes
levels.introduction:
Mathlib composes homeomorphisms with `e.trans f`: first `e`, then `f`. The theorem `Homeomorph.trans_apply` tells Lean how that bundled composition acts on a point.

Apply the named library theorem explicitly. This makes the mathematical API visible instead of letting simplification hide it.
levels.conclusion: You now have the basic coordinate-change algebra: continuity, inverse continuity, round trips, and composition.
hints: Use the fully qualified theorem name.

worlds.title: Open partial homeomorphisms
worlds.introduction:
# A chart is deliberately partial

A globe cannot be flattened by one global homeomorphism. A chart only maps an open patch of the manifold to an open patch of a model space.

Mathlib represents that object as `OpenPartialHomeomorph X Y`. It has a `source`, a `target`, local continuity, and inverse laws that require a proof that the point lies in the relevant patch.

levels.title: The source is open
levels.introduction:
The domain of a local chart is not arbitrary. `OpenPartialHomeomorph` stores the theorem `open_source : IsOpen e.source`.

Read the target first: Lean wants proof that a set is open. Then inspect the bundled chart for a field with exactly that type.
levels.conclusion: Open chart domains ensure that every point in the patch still has room for local analysis.
levels.statement:
local_chart_source_open {X : Type u} {Y : Type v} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (e : OpenPartialHomeomorph X Y) : IsOpen e.source

levels.title: Continuity on the patch
levels.introduction:
A partial chart is only required to behave continuously on its source. Mathlib states that precisely with `ContinuousOn e e.source`.

Unlock `OpenPartialHomeomorph.continuousOn` by projecting it from `e`.
levels.conclusion: The type distinguishes global continuity from continuity restricted to the chart domain.
levels.statement:
local_chart_continuous {X : Type u} {Y : Type v} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (e : OpenPartialHomeomorph X Y) : ContinuousOn e e.source

levels.title: A source point reaches the target
levels.introduction:
Now membership matters. The chart is a total Lean function syntactically, but its geometric guarantees are conditional on `hx : x ∈ e.source`.

Feed that evidence to `OpenPartialHomeomorph.map_source`.
levels.conclusion: Mathlib uses explicit source-membership hypotheses to keep partial geometry honest.
levels.statement:
local_chart_maps_source {X : Type u} {Y : Type v} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (e : OpenPartialHomeomorph X Y) (x : X) (hx : x ∈ e.source) : e x ∈ e.target
hints: Apply `e.map_source` first; its remaining input is the source-membership proof.
Then close the new goal with `exact hx`.

levels.title: A local round trip
levels.introduction:
The global round-trip theorem from world 1 needed no side condition. A partial homeomorphism needs `hx`: only points in the chart source are promised to return.

Use the actual local inverse law `OpenPartialHomeomorph.left_inv`.
levels.conclusion: This is the equation a coordinate chart must satisfy on its patch.
levels.statement:
local_chart_round_trip {X : Type u} {Y : Type v} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (e : OpenPartialHomeomorph X Y) (x : X) (hx : x ∈ e.source) : e.symm (e x) = x

worlds.title: Charted spaces and atlases
worlds.introduction:
# Mathlib's chart data

`ChartedSpace H M` says that the topological space `M` has charts into the model space `H`. Its data consists of an `atlas H M` and a preferred `chartAt H x` for every point.

The class deliberately stores both the covering facts needed constantly in later proofs: the point lies in its preferred chart's source, and that chart belongs to the atlas.

levels.title: Every point has a chart
levels.introduction:
The chosen chart `chartAt H x` is useful because Mathlib guarantees that it contains `x`. The public theorem is `mem_chart_source H x`.

Notice how the instance argument `[ChartedSpace H M]` supplies an entire atlas without appearing as an ordinary named hypothesis.
levels.conclusion: You have proved the local-cover condition for one arbitrary point using the real `ChartedSpace` class.
levels.statement:
point_mem_preferred_chart {H : Type u} {M : Type v} [TopologicalSpace H] [TopologicalSpace M]
    [ChartedSpace H M] (x : M) : x ∈ (chartAt H x).source

levels.title: The chosen chart belongs to the atlas
levels.introduction:
A preferred chart is not extra data floating beside the atlas. `chart_mem_atlas H x` proves it is one of the atlas charts.

This connection is used when smooth compatibility is known for atlas members.
levels.conclusion: The class ties pointwise chart selection back to the global atlas.
levels.statement:
preferred_chart_mem_atlas {H : Type u} {M : Type v} [TopologicalSpace H] [TopologicalSpace M]
    [ChartedSpace H M] (x : M) : chartAt H x ∈ atlas H M

levels.title: The point reaches coordinate space
levels.introduction:
Combine the selected chart with its source-membership guarantee: the coordinate value `chartAt H x x` lies in the chart's target.

Mathlib has already packaged that composition as `mem_chart_target H x`. Use it rather than replaying `map_source` manually.
levels.conclusion: Named theorems let later formalization operate at the manifold level instead of unpacking chart fields each time.
levels.statement:
preferred_chart_maps_to_target {H : Type u} {M : Type v} [TopologicalSpace H] [TopologicalSpace M]
    [ChartedSpace H M] (x : M) : chartAt H x x ∈ (chartAt H x).target
hints: Use the newly introduced theorem `mem_chart_target H x`.

levels.title: A chart source is a neighborhood
levels.introduction:
Open sets containing `x` are neighborhoods of `x`. Mathlib's filter notation `𝓝 x` records all neighborhoods at once.

`chart_source_mem_nhds H x` combines openness of the chart source with `mem_chart_source`.
levels.conclusion: This is a genuinely topological formulation of “the chart is valid near the point.”
levels.statement:
preferred_chart_source_is_neighborhood {H : Type u} {M : Type v} [TopologicalSpace H] [TopologicalSpace M]
    [ChartedSpace H M] (x : M) : (chartAt H x).source ∈ 𝓝 x

levels.title: The preferred charts cover
levels.introduction:
The pointwise condition becomes a global cover: union all preferred chart sources and obtain all of `M`.

Mathlib exposes this theorem as `iUnion_source_chartAt H M`. It is the atlas-covering idea stated with actual sets and indexed unions.
levels.conclusion: You have reached the central theorem of a charted space: its selected local coordinate patches cover the whole space.
levels.statement:
preferred_charts_cover {H : Type u} {M : Type v} [TopologicalSpace H] [TopologicalSpace M]
    [ChartedSpace H M] : (⋃ x : M, (chartAt H x).source) = (Set.univ : Set M)

worlds.title: Identity and product charts
worlds.introduction:
# Instances build geometry for you

Mathlib supplies canonical `ChartedSpace` instances. Every topological space is charted over itself by the identity chart. Products of charted spaces are charted by products of their component charts.

This world makes typeclass inference visible: the same notation `chartAt` selects different structured instances from the types in the goal.

levels.title: A model charts itself by identity
levels.introduction:
For the canonical `ChartedSpace H H` instance, the preferred chart is the identity open partial homeomorphism.

Prove the exact Mathlib theorem `chartAt_self_eq`.
levels.conclusion: The model space itself is the simplest charted space: one global identity chart is enough.
levels.statement:
self_chart_is_identity {H : Type u} [TopologicalSpace H] (x : H) :
    chartAt H x = OpenPartialHomeomorph.refl H
hints: The theorem has all arguments implicit: `exact chartAt_self_eq`.

levels.title: Its atlas contains only identity
levels.introduction:
The self-charted atlas is the singleton containing the identity chart. Mathlib states membership in that atlas as an equivalence.

Split the `↔` with `constructor`, then use the forward and backward directions of `chartedSpaceSelf_atlas`.
levels.conclusion: You can now see both components of the canonical instance: the selected chart and the atlas it belongs to.
levels.statement:
self_atlas_only_identity {H : Type u} [TopologicalSpace H] (e : OpenPartialHomeomorph H H) :
    e ∈ atlas H H ↔ e = OpenPartialHomeomorph.refl H
levels.solution:
constructor
· intro h
  exact chartedSpaceSelf_atlas.mp h
· intro h
  exact chartedSpaceSelf_atlas.mpr h
hints: Use `constructor` to prove the two directions of the equivalence.
In each direction, introduce the hypothesis and use `.mp` or `.mpr` from `chartedSpaceSelf_atlas`.

levels.title: A product chart is a product
levels.introduction:
The model for a product manifold is `ModelProd H H'`. Its preferred chart is built by pairing the preferred charts of the two factors.

This is not an analogy: `prodChartedSpace_chartAt` is the definitional theorem used throughout Mathlib.
levels.conclusion: Product manifolds inherit coordinates componentwise.
levels.statement:
product_chart_is_product {H : Type u} {H' : Type u'} {M : Type v} {M' : Type v'}
    [TopologicalSpace H] [TopologicalSpace H'] [TopologicalSpace M] [TopologicalSpace M']
    [ChartedSpace H M] [ChartedSpace H' M'] (x : M × M') :
    chartAt (ModelProd H H') x = (chartAt H x.1).prod (chartAt H' x.2)

levels.title: The product point is covered
levels.introduction:
The general covering theorem `mem_chart_source` also works for the product instance. Lean infers that instance from the model and manifold types in the goal.

Instantiate the theorem with `ModelProd H H'` and the pair `(x, y)`.
levels.conclusion: Typeclass composition has constructed and verified the product charted space for you.
levels.statement:
product_point_mem_chart_source {H : Type u} {H' : Type u'} {M : Type v} {M' : Type v'}
    [TopologicalSpace H] [TopologicalSpace H'] [TopologicalSpace M] [TopologicalSpace M']
    [ChartedSpace H M] [ChartedSpace H' M'] (x : M) (y : M') :
    (x, y) ∈ (chartAt (ModelProd H H') (x, y)).source
levels.solution: simpa only using (mem_chart_source (ModelProd H H') (x, y))
hints: Specialize the earlier theorem to the product model and pair.
Use `simpa only using (mem_chart_source (ModelProd H H') (x, y))`.

worlds.title: Smooth manifolds
worlds.introduction:
# From charts to compatible calculus

`ChartedSpace` only supplies topological charts. Mathlib's `IsManifold I n M` adds compatibility with a differentiability groupoid determined by:

- a scalar field `𝕜`,
- a normed model vector space `E`,
- a `ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E H`, and
- a differentiability order `n : WithTop ℕ∞`.

Here `n = 0` is topological, `n = ∞` is smooth, and `n = ω` is analytic.

levels.title: The model space is a manifold
levels.introduction:
Every model with corners is itself a manifold of every differentiability order. Mathlib registers this as an instance, so the tactic `infer_instance` can synthesize the proof from the types alone.

This is your first deliberate use of the typeclass system as a proof engine.
levels.conclusion: The base case for manifold constructions is now in place: the model space carries its canonical manifold structure.
levels.statement:
model_space_is_manifold {𝕜 : Type u} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
    {E : Type v} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]
    {H : Type w} [TopologicalSpace H] (I : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E H) (n : WithTop ℕ∞) :
    IsManifold I n H
hints: The result is a registered instance.

levels.title: More smoothness implies less
levels.introduction:
If every transition map is `C^n`, it is also `C^m` whenever `m ≤ n`.

Mathlib packages the downgrade as `IsManifold.of_le`. Supply the inequality `hmn`; the existing `IsManifold I n M` instance is found automatically.
levels.conclusion: Smoothness levels form a hierarchy, and the theorem records the direction precisely.
levels.statement:
manifold_of_higher_smoothness {𝕜 : Type u} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
    {E : Type v} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]
    {H : Type w} [TopologicalSpace H] {I : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E H}
    {M : Type u'} [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M]
    {m n : WithTop ℕ∞} [IsManifold I n M] (hmn : m ≤ n) : IsManifold I m M

levels.title: Smooth implies topological
levels.introduction:
A smooth manifold is, in particular, a topological manifold relative to the same model with corners.

Mathlib has an instance that applies the smoothness hierarchy automatically. Let `infer_instance` find the chain.
levels.conclusion: The differentiability parameter is real formal structure: Lean has derived the `C^0` manifold from the `C^∞` one.
levels.statement:
smooth_manifold_is_topological {𝕜 : Type u} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
    {E : Type v} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]
    {H : Type w} [TopologicalSpace H] {I : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E H}
    {M : Type u'} [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M]
    [IsManifold I ∞ M] : IsManifold I 0 M
hints: This implication is registered with typeclass inference.

levels.title: Products preserve manifolds
levels.introduction:
The product of two `C^n` manifolds is a `C^n` manifold. Mathlib combines the product chart instance from the last world with the product model-with-corners and a compatibility proof.

The declaration is registered as the instance `IsManifold.prod`. Apply that actual Mathlib declaration to the two manifold types.
levels.conclusion: This construction formally covers spaces such as the torus viewed as a product of two circles, once the circle instances are supplied.
levels.statement:
product_of_manifolds {𝕜 : Type u} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
    {E : Type v} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]
    {E' : Type v'} [NormedAddCommGroup E'] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E']
    {H : Type w} [TopologicalSpace H] {H' : Type*} [TopologicalSpace H']
    {I : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E H} {I' : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E' H'}
    {M : Type u'} [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M]
    {M' : Type*} [TopologicalSpace M'] [ChartedSpace H' M']
    (n : WithTop ℕ∞) [IsManifold I n M] [IsManifold I' n M'] :
    IsManifold (I.prod I') n (M × M')
hints: The product instance takes the two manifold types explicitly.

worlds.title: Tangent spaces and the tangent bundle
worlds.introduction:
# Dependent geometry

For a manifold modelled on a normed vector space `E`, Mathlib defines `TangentSpace I x` at every point `x`. The total tangent bundle `TangentBundle I M` is a dependent pair: a base point together with a tangent vector in that point's fiber.

This final world moves from propositions about structures to constructing values of dependent types.

levels.title: The zero tangent vector
levels.introduction:
Every tangent space inherits an additive commutative group structure from the model vector space. Therefore it has a zero vector.

The expected type tells Lean which `0` you mean. Supply it with `exact 0`.
levels.conclusion: You have constructed a real value of Mathlib's `TangentSpace I x`, not merely proved that a tangent vector “exists.”
levels.statement:
tangent_zero {𝕜 : Type u} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
    {E : Type v} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]
    {H : Type w} [TopologicalSpace H] (I : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E H)
    {M : Type u'} [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M] (x : M) : TangentSpace I x
hints: The tangent space has a zero instance.

levels.title: Package a tangent vector
levels.introduction:
A point of the tangent bundle is a dependent pair `⟨x, v⟩`: the fiber type of `v` depends on the chosen base point `x`.

Lean knows `x` implicitly from the type of `v`, so construct the pair directly.
levels.conclusion: The tangent bundle is now concrete: its elements carry both location and direction.
levels.statement:
tangent_vector_as_bundle_point {𝕜 : Type u} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
    {E : Type v} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]
    {H : Type w} [TopologicalSpace H] (I : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E H)
    {M : Type u'} [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M]
    {x : M} (v : TangentSpace I x) : TangentBundle I M

levels.title: Project the base point
levels.introduction:
The first projection of `⟨x, v⟩` computes to `x`. This equality holds by definitional reduction, so `rfl` closes it.

Here `rfl` is proving a fact about a dependent bundle representation, not an invented natural-number example.
levels.conclusion: Definitional equality makes the bundle projection computationally transparent.
levels.statement:
tangent_bundle_base {𝕜 : Type u} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
    {E : Type v} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]
    {H : Type w} [TopologicalSpace H] (I : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E H)
    {M : Type u'} [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M]
    {x : M} (v : TangentSpace I x) : (⟨x, v⟩ : TangentBundle I M).1 = x

levels.title: A zero section, point by point
levels.introduction:
Finish by constructing a tangent-bundle point over an arbitrary base point. Use the course theorem `tangent_zero I x` that you proved in this world, package it with `x`, and prove that the first projection is `x`.

This is a pointwise form of the zero section of the tangent bundle.
levels.conclusion: You have crossed the full ladder: bundled homeomorphisms → partial charts → atlases → smooth-manifold instances → dependent tangent-bundle values.
levels.statement:
tangent_bundle_has_zero {𝕜 : Type u} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
    {E : Type v} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]
    {H : Type w} [TopologicalSpace H] (I : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E H)
    {M : Type u'} [TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M] (x : M) :
    ∃ p : TangentBundle I M, p.1 = x
hints: Use `refine` with the witness `⟨x, tangent_zero I x⟩` and leave its base equation as `?_`.
